If Paris is worth a Mass, this villa isn't worth a penny.

And yet, it was precisely for one penny a year that Benito Mussolini rented Villa Torlonia, one of Rome's most extraordinary residences.

Born as a symbol of the rise of the Torlonia family, who had grown wealthy through banking, the villa was transformed in the 19th century by some of the most important architects of the time (including Valadier) into a place capable of astonishing with gardens, temples, obelisks, and spectacular architecture.

Frescoes, marble, and a breathtaking ballroom: every room of the Casino Nobile was designed to celebrate the power and wealth of the Torlonias.
A beautiful park in the center of Rome, very large and full of green spaces for both children and adults, a true oasis of relaxation that combines history and culture.
We went to the Festival of Flavours, very nice, well organised, a very pleasant situation.

The grounds are beautiful, and the villa itself is well-maintained. A visit inside conveys the building's rich history. Upstairs, you can admire an exhibition of paintings that perfectly complement the overall ensemble.

Villa Torlonia is a magnificent park, ideal for exploring starting from Via Spallanzani, convenient for accessing eateries like La Limonaia.
​Truly fascinating historical and cultural itineraries unfold within:
​The Casino Nobile, a majestic manor house with its sumptuous Ballroom.
​The Casina delle Civette, a fairytale and eclectic building famous for its magnificent Art Nouveau stained glass windows.
​The Serra Moresca, with its exotic and colorful details inspired by the Alhambra.
​The Casino dei Principi, the nearby Limonaia, and the interactive Technotown area.
​The underground tour of the anti-aircraft bunker.
​A stroll immersed in greenery that combines architecture, nature, and art in a truly unique atmosphere.
Great place, some water sources available as well.
We bought a combined ticket for Villa Torlonia, the owl house and the Moorish greenhouse, all well kept.

They really need to put up better signage. This is a huge area- much larger than I expected. We came on the bus and it was a 800m trudge just to get onto the grounds. We entered the obvious park area and had no idea which way to go because of 0 signage. The first building we came to was locked up tight. I finally recognized the Civette. On entry, the lady said we needed to go to yet another building to buy a ticket. My feet said no and I stood there and bought an online ticket. Note that each building requires a separate ticket. Buying the tickets together is cheaper than individually as you'll see on their website. I will review the Civette elsewhere but don't underestimate the size and scale of the area. To add to the misery, the estate is enclosed with a 20 foot tall pointy top wrought iron fence so there is no going out to the surrounding streets except through their designated openings. There don't seem to be bus stops particularly close by, and the metro is a long ways away. It's a really nice area away from tourists, but unless you are here several weeks, I would give it a pass.

This magnificent villa and its surrounding buildings have been restored to their former glory thanks to the extensive restoration carried out a few years ago.

The only drawback is the state of preservation of the gardens and unprotected architectural elements—a common problem in Rome.
A wonderful collection of art nouveau sketches and stain glass. The building alone is a work of art.
Fantastic park full of history and natural areas for the whole family
Very interesting historical place famous for its stained glass windows

When I went in 2022, I loved it. I returned in September 2026 and was extremely disappointed. The park is completely neglected. It's a shame. They charge an entrance fee to enter the Village. It's a pity because I remembered it being a very beautiful place. I hope they take better care of it.
Nice big park

If you are a resident of Paris, this museum, like those in Rome, is free. This villa, while famous for the visit of Mussolini (whose presence sometimes casts a shadow over the experience), displays works by painters of the Roman school on the top floor, creating a small art gallery. Thematic divisions within each room—Egyptian, ancient, Greek—are common in these Roman villas.

Villa Torlonia is an eclectic and less touristy historic oasis in the heart of Rome, famous for its manicured parks, Art Nouveau architecture, and its complex 20th-century history. It was Benito Mussolini's Roman residence between 1925 and 1943; beneath the park is an anti-aircraft bunker. Perfect for a quiet stroll, for families, and for lovers of art and alternative architecture.

Villa Torlonia is an elegant historic park in Rome, located at Via Nomentana 70, and was once the residence of Mussolini. The most interesting features are the Casina delle Civette (Cow's House), the Casino Nobile (Noble Casino), the gardens, and the air-raid shelters.

The first owners were the Pamphili family, later succeeded by a Cardinal. Both families used the land for agriculture. It then passed into the hands of the Torlonia family, a Jewish banker who leased it to Mussolini for one lira a year. After Mussolini's death, the Torlonia family retained ownership until the City of Rome opened it as a public park for the enjoyment of its citizens.
Always very beautiful
The museums and buildings are interesting, picturesque, and artistically significant, but the Villa, as a public park, is quite run down.

A fascinating place where history reigns supreme. Beautifully restored, almost all of the park's various buildings can be visited with a single ticket. Truly not to be missed, not least for the splendid collections of paintings housed within, as well as the temporary exhibitions.
Don't go. Don't worry, there's nothing there.

Large park that could use some maintenance here and there. There are 4 buildings that you can visit for a fee. Besides the beautiful historical rooms, there are also all kinds of paintings. Not all of this was to our taste.
Free museums for Rome residents, excluding the bunker (guided tours must be booked in advance)
We hope it will be kept better and better

A real discovery with a lovely park to stroll around. The Casina delle Civette is wonderful. It's best to set aside a couple of hours and also visit the villa's interior (including Mussolini's bunker). In the summer, various events take place in the gardens or in the theater.

We went to Villa Torlonia during the Night of the Museums. There were people there, but not as many as in the historic center.
Entrance to the Bunker requires a reservation; it doesn't count toward the MIC Card. Other admissions are valid, but you can check them online.

Unfortunately, the park is still closed from 5:50 AM until around 6:30 AM. Seen from the expensive entrance gates, it's truly a beautiful green heart in the middle of the city. A lovely walk around, anyway!
A real dream!!! 💖 …
A place rich in history and beauty, also suitable for children and quadrupeds

Villa Torlonia is one of Rome's most unique historic villas, originally an aristocratic residence and transformed over time into a complex rich in architecture, art, and history.

The villa was built between the late 18th and early 19th centuries as the property of the Torlonia family, one of the richest and most influential families of the time. Over time, especially under the leadership of Giovanni Torlonia and his heirs, the estate was expanded and transformed into a truly monumental villa.

English-style gardens, scenic buildings, and stately spaces were created, in keeping with the 19th-century taste that blended nature, architecture, and decoration.

A complex rich in buildings

During the 19th and early 20th centuries, the villa was enriched with numerous structures:

* the Casino Nobile
* the Casina delle Civette
* the Serra Moorsca
* the stables and other service buildings

Each building reflects different tastes, from neoclassical to Art Nouveau to "exotic" style, making the complex highly diverse and scenic.

The Mussolini Period:

During the 20th century, Villa Torlonia also assumed an important historical role: it became the residence of Benito Mussolini and his family from 1925 to 1943. During this period, the bunker and other underground structures were also built.

After the war, the villa was returned to the City of Rome and gradually opened to the public. Today, it is a large historical park and museum, open to visitors, where nature and architecture coexist.

Villa Torlonia is today a unique place in Rome: not just a park, but a journey through the city's history, recounting centuries of transformations between aristocracy, art, and historical memory.

Casino Nobile was nice, but I didn't like the other casinos as much. The restaurant was only for guests with reservations.

Otherwise, they only served sandwiches and sweets.

Villa Torlonia is one of those places in Rome that always surprises, even when you think you know everything about the city. Strolling through the park is an experience that combines history, nature, and an almost suspended atmosphere, allowing you to momentarily forget the frenetic pace of the capital. The tree-lined avenues, manicured green spaces, and the play of light filtering through the trees create a relaxing and pleasant atmosphere in every season.

The architecture within the complex is an extraordinary added value. From the Casino Nobile to the Casino dei Principi, to the famous Casina delle Civette, each building tells a story and offers unique views, perfect for those who love art, photography, or simply beauty. The Casina delle Civette, in particular, with its stained-glass windows and fairytale-like style, is a little gem definitely worth a visit.

The park is clean, well-maintained, and ideal for both a leisurely stroll and a few hours of relaxation in the open air. Even at the busiest times, you can still find quiet corners to enjoy the peace and quiet.

Villa Torlonia is a precious oasis in the heart of Rome, a place that impeccably combines culture, nature, and charm. A well-deserved five stars.

The villa and its adjoining structures are well-maintained and easily accessible. I expected the interiors to be richer in artifacts and objects. Unfortunately, we Romans are accustomed to too much, and a museum like this feels almost bare.
We thank the Torlonias

A historic site worth a visit. It's easily accessible by public transport.
The enormous park within the walls is ideal for strolling, relaxing, and picnicking.
The historic museum buildings (Casino Nobile and Casina delle Civette) are architecturally stunning, enriched by museums, stained glass windows, and prestigious areas such as the Limonaia and the Serra Moresca.
Poorly maintained. The Lugano city council should be called in to teach them how to enhance parks and more.
A calm and peaceful experience
Great park with the annual Franconian Beer Festival
A very beautiful park with numerous historical sites. Relatively few visitors and none of the usual "big city phenomena" (no homeless people or drug dealers).

A fascinating complex, it immerses visitors in another era; the noble house is truly spectacular, even on the outside, thanks to the white Corinthian colonnaded portico; the little house of the owls is curious and in Art Nouveau style; the stained-glass windows, when lit properly, sparkle with a thousand colors and are works of great ingenuity, the same goes for the Moorish greenhouse and the graceful Moorish tower, which features two rooms: the kitchens and the brightly decorated dining room, plus a clever engineering trick that allowed the round table to "rise" to the fully laid floor... it must have been surprising and spectacular.
I didn't give it 5 stars only because I wasn't able to visit the theater (reservations are required online, with a maximum of 25 people per shift, not every day), the stables (which are entrusted to a science center and are closed), or the Casino dei Principi, with its splendid sphinxes at the entrance, because it was closed for installations. No one told me what they were. The park also features obelisks and a beautiful decorative pond, plus an underground one. However, being a public park, it was very crowded, and there were even ladies in bathing suits sunbathing. The day was hot, but a little more decor wouldn't have been out of place. This prevented me from enjoying the architectural symmetries and the park complex. I was also disappointed that the historic lemon house has been converted into a restaurant; convenient perhaps for tourists and Romans, but in my opinion, a shame.
Overall, a very satisfying visit; Recommended for art and history lovers (splendid paintings on the upper floor of the Casino Nobile... not to be missed) and suitable for those who love observing details.
Stunning location for FrankenBierFest.
Enchanting!
Stunning. Beautiful museum. Unique little house, interesting greenhouse, but I haven't seen the theater. I've booked a visit to the bunker villa.

A beautiful green space near the center of Rome, probably less beautiful than the more famous Villa Borghese and Villa Pamphili, but worth a visit. Unfortunately, since it was a Monday, I wasn't able to visit the Serra Moresca, the Casina delle Civette, and other buildings. I'll be back.
Beautiful but very neglected. We are far from how these Italian excellences should be cared for.
Beautiful villa where you can enjoy some spring sunshine
Very nice!
Beautiful place to rest ❤️
Very beautiful but perhaps a little more maintenance and better organization of museum opening hours.

A magical place with a beautiful atmosphere and is very well-kept. M*ssolini and his family also lived there. It was built by the Tortona family. There are beautiful museums and even a bunker worth visiting. Recommended.
Very beautiful park, with very beautiful buildings

Villa Torlonia is a fairly large park with three sites to visit: the Casina Nobile, where Mussolini lived with his family; the Casa della Civette (House of the Owls), with its magnificent stained-glass windows, floors, and ceilings; and the Serra Orientale (Eastern Greenhouse) Pavilion, with its beautiful stained-glass windows and ornamental plants. A single ticket includes three admissions. There are other sites to visit, including a children's area with games and technical experiences, and a nearby café/restaurant.
One of the best villa to see in Rome it has a lot of great things to see

A splendid villa, meticulously maintained with vast gardens to explore in a marvelous setting, immersed in art at every turn. I had the opportunity to visit the Casina delle Civette, a truly enchanting place, meticulously maintained both inside and out, and beautifully restored. It's definitely worth a more in-depth visit. I was there on Saturday afternoon for a brief visit, but I'd definitely like to return to visit the Bunker and the Library, which I believe require reservations, and last but not least, the greenhouse, which unfortunately we found closed because we didn't arrive in time. A villa definitely worth visiting.

Villa Torlonia: a Roman jewel 🏛️🌿😊
​I took advantage of the first Sunday of the month (a wonderful initiative that allows free admission to Rome's civic museums) to finally visit the Villa Torlonia complex.
Even though the bunker wasn't open to visitors during my stay, the experience was still incredible and I was fascinated...
​La Casina delle Civette: It seems straight out of a fairytale. The stained-glass windows and esoteric details are mesmerizing. It's a one-of-a-kind example of Art Nouveau style that will leave you speechless.
​Il Casino Nobile: The elegance of the interiors and the richness of the decorations are breathtaking. You can feel the history at every step, and the care taken in the museum displays is truly remarkable.
​Il Parco: Even just strolling through the villa's avenues is rejuvenating. It's a peaceful haven away from the chaos of the city, perfect for enjoying the architectural beauty while surrounded by greenery.
Villa Torlonia is a must-see for anyone who loves art, architecture, and historic parks. It gets top marks! ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐
It’s a small-medium size park for everyone. Lots of birds, and singing out loud. Especially those green parrots.Grass was well pruned.
